10081-the-boy-allies-at-jutland-or-the-g:
Ensign Robert L. Drake's 1917 boys' book sends the Boy Allies to Jutland, the greatest naval battle of history, as its subtitle claims. The story opens aboard H.M.S. Queen Mary, and follows the young heroes through the North Sea clash of British and German fleets.

Drake, author of many Boy Allies volumes, writes fast, patriotic adventure for boys, with ships, guns, and narrow escapes. The Jutland book lets young readers stand on a battle-cruiser's deck in the Great War's largest sea fight. It is stirring, straightforward, and unashamedly on the side of the fleet.
10878-the-mule-a-treatise-on-the-breedin:
Harvey Riley, superintendent of the government corral at Washington, published The Mule in 1867 as a treatise on breeding, training, and uses. Riley argues that no animal is more useful or willing, yet none is so abused or so little cared for. Prejudice has made the mule plod through life against ignorant opinion, though in war and peace he serves faithfully.

The book seeks reform in breeding, care, and kind treatment, asking what the mule most needs from man. Its advice covers feeding, handling, and work. Farmers, teamsters, and animal lovers get a practical, humane manual from the age of horse-drawn America.
12745-the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-:
Edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, this volume of The World's Greatest Books surveys ancient and medieval history through short summaries. Egypt, the Jews, Greece, and Rome open the book, with Maspero, Josephus, Herodotus, Thucydides, Xenophon, Caesar, Tacitus, Sallust, Gibbon, and Mommsen all sampled. Medieval Europe, England, and Egypt follow.

A famous passage retells Xenophon's Greeks crying The sea! The sea! on reaching the Black Sea after long marching. Each summary gives plot and argument in brief, so readers can grasp a great history fast. The volume works as a gateway to histories too long to tackle whole.
13118-profiles-from-china-sketches-in-fr:
Eunice Tietjens's 1917 Profiles from China gathers free-verse sketches of people and things seen in the interior, dedicated to her mother. Contents run from Cormorants, A Scholar, and The Story Teller to The Well, The Abandoned God, The Bridge, and The Shop. Later sections cover New China, iron works, and Chinese New Year, with echoes from tourists in Hong Kong and Canton.

Tietjens writes of a servant whose bound feet thump dully on the floor, instep broken upward, toes folded under. She also notes two sounds above a city's cry: the mission bell each hour, and the factory whistle morning and evening. Shifts run ten hours by day and fourteen by night. The poems are sharp, spare portraits of old and new China side by side.
13213-the-night-before-christmas-and-oth:
Published in Chicago in 1903 by W. B. Conkey, this illustrated collection for children opens with The Night Before Christmas, where not a creature stirs, not even a mouse, and stockings hang by the chimney with care. Other tales include The Night After Christmas, Santa Claus Does Not Forget, The Fairy Christmas, and The Dolls' Christmas Party. The book is made for reading aloud at the season.

One story tells of lonely girls who let a hungry boy, Guido, share their table, and of parents who return by train to find their darlings happy. Guido never goes hungry again, and calls it a fairy Christmas. Another shows tableaux of Sleeping Beauty, Red Riding Hood, and Mother Hubbard, arranged by Miss Marcelle. The collection is sweet, simple, and full of old holiday charm.
15391-american-eloquence-volume-1-studie:
Edited by Alexander Johnston and reedited by James Albert Woodburn, this first volume of American Eloquence studies political history through speeches. Sections cover colonialism and the Constitution, constitutional government, the rise of democracy, and the rise of nationality. Otis, Henry, Adams, Hamilton, and Madison lead the set.

Gallatin, Ames, Jefferson, Randolph, Quincy, Clay, Hayne, Webster, Calhoun, and Benton follow, with portraits from paintings by Trumbull and Longacre. The volume lets readers hear American argument in its own words. Students of rhetoric and history will find it a rich, well-chosen anthology.
15392-american-eloquence-volume-2-studie:
Alexander Johnston edited this second volume of American Eloquence, reedited by James Albert Woodburn, covering the anti-slavery struggle. It prints full speeches, with portraits, from the Senate, the House, and public halls. The volume is one of four tracing American political history through its great orators.

Speeches open with Rufus King and William Pinkney on the Missouri struggle in 1820. They move on to Wendell Phillips on the murder of Lovejoy, and John Quincy Adams on war power over slavery. Calhoun, Webster, and Clay debate the Compromise of 1850, and Sumner urges repeal of the Fugitive Slave Law. Read in order, the speeches show a nation arguing, in public, toward a crisis it could not talk away.
15393-american-eloquence-volume-3-studie:
This third volume of American Eloquence continues the anti-slavery struggle and turns to secession, in speeches edited by Johnston and Woodburn. Chase, Everett, and Douglas debate the Kansas-Nebraska Bill in the Senate in 1854, while Sumner speaks on the crime against Kansas in 1856. Brooks answers on the Sumner assault.

Judah Benjamin's property doctrine and later secession speeches complete the arc from debate to break. The volume shows American eloquence at its most fateful, as words hardened into war. Students of the Civil War era will find the speeches powerful, revealing, and essential reading.
15394-american-eloquence-volume-4-studie:
This fourth and final volume of American Eloquence, edited by Alexander Johnston and reedited by James Albert Woodburn, covers Civil War and Reconstruction, then free trade, finance, and civil service reform. It prints the speeches as delivered, from inaugural addresses to Senate debates, so readers can follow arguments in the speakers' own words.

Lincoln's first and second inaugurals and the Gettysburg Address anchor the war section, beside Jefferson Davis, Alexander Stephens, and debates on insurrection and reconstruction. Later parts weigh trade and money questions that shaped the postwar republic. The volume closes a set that teaches American history through oratory, letting clashing voices, North and South, make the case for their causes.
16106-what-is-free-trade-an-adaptation-o:
Emile Walter, calling himself a worker, adapted Frederic Bastiat's witty French essays on trade for American readers in 1867. Putnam published the book in New York, with twenty chapters that take Bastiat's arguments and reset them for the United States. Plenty and scarcity, taxes on home goods, the balance of trade, and duties that favor one group open the discussion.

Later chapters ask plain questions: does protection raise wages, does it make a nation independent, and what happens when rivers, railroads, and prices are all tangled in the same rules? Bastiat's style is short, sharp, and full of parables, and Walter keeps that bite. Readers new to trade debates will find a clear, lively case for free exchange.
17483-the-olden-time-series-vol-3-new-en:
Henry M. Brooks prepared this third volume of the Olden-Time Series, on New England Sunday gleanings, in a handy sixteenmo format sold at fifty cents. Brooks notes a growing popular taste for quaint and curious memories of ye olden time. His materials came chiefly from old newspapers of Boston and Salem, sources not easily reached by ordinary readers.

Brooks does not claim to write formal history, but his gleanings hold much material for history, combined and presented for pleasure. Readers get Sunday customs, churchgoing, and town life in old New England, in short, readable pieces. The volume suits readers of local history and of antiquarian charm.
18517-anti-achitophel-1682-three-verse-r:
Harold Whitmore Jones edited this 1961 volume of three verse replies to John Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel of 1682. The three poems are Elkanah Settle's Absalom Senior, an anonymous Poetical Reflections, and Samuel Pordage's Azaria and Hushai. Jones prints them as facsimiles from copies in the British Museum and the Florida library, with a long introduction.

His notes sort out who wrote what, when each piece first appeared, and why Settle's poem stands as the strongest answer to Dryden. The anonymous poem, long tied to Buckingham on thin proof, gets a careful fresh look. Scholars of Restoration satire will find this a handy source book.
19969-the-moving-picture-girls-at-oak-fa:
Laura Lee Hope's Moving Picture Girls at Oak Farm appeared in 1914. A motley crowd stands in the Hoboken train shed one June morning. Travelers pause to stare at the gathering twice over. The moving picture company is off to film rural plays at Oak Farm. Queer happenings while taking those plays fill the subtitle. The girls of the company are sisters Ruth and Alice DeVere.

The Moving Picture Girls series chased the new film industry. Its heroines acted before cameras when movies were young. Oak Farm gives them hayfields, barns, and a mystery. Stratemeyer syndicate plotting keeps chapters brisk and bright. The book preserves early film-making as girls' adventure. Cameras, in 1914, were still marvelous machines.
21237-the-bush-boys-history-and-adventur:
Hendrik Von Bloom was a boor, Captain Mayne Reid begins. He then explains that at the Cape a boor is simply a Dutch farmer, no insult meant. Von Bloom farms in Britain's Cape Colony with his family. Their history and adventures make the book.

Reid uses the tale to introduce the mammals, birds, and snakes of South Africa to young English readers. Afrikaans words and phrases from the Boer farmers season the talk, as Spanish did in his Mexican tales. Tense moments build one after another as the family meets the dangers of bush life, and Reid keeps readers guessing how each scrape will end.
22081-parodies-of-ballad-criticism-1711-:
Parodies of Ballad Criticism, 1711–1787 studies a curious corner of literary history. Its subject is the flood of mock criticism that followed Joseph Addison's famous Spectator essays on the ballad Chevy Chase. Addison had praised the rough old ballad as true poetry. Wits answered with parodies, fake scholarship, and jokes at the critics' expense.

The study tracks those parodies across most of the eighteenth century. It shows how arguments about ballads became arguments about taste itself. Scholars of the period quarrelled over nature, rules, and the value of popular song. This scholarly volume preserves the lighter side of that quarrel, where laughter did the work of criticism.
22655-nelka-mrs-helen-de-smirnoff-moukha:
Michael Moukhanoff wrote Nelka, a biography of Mrs. Helen de Smirnoff Moukhanoff, whose life ran from 1878 to 1963. The catalog record gives no year. A family biography of this kind follows its subject through the vanished world of imperial Russia and the upheavals that scattered its people.

The sample reaches into the family's American ties, recalling a kinsman who stood against slavery in the free-soil movement. He was a friend of Abraham Lincoln and of President Grant, and held posts from both. He served as minister to Venezuela and ambassador to Brazil. His brothers, by contrast, were southern Democrats. Such connections lace the life story. The book preserves one family's path across empires, revolutions, and oceans.
25212-a-glossary-of-provincial-words-phr:
A Glossary of Provincial Words and Phrases in Use in Somersetshire, published in 1873, records the dialect of an English county before it faded. Wadham Pigott Williams, vicar of Bishop's Hull, compiled it with the late William Arthur Jones, and R. C. A. Prior wrote the introduction.

Entries run from A, meaning he, through words for farm tools, weather, mining, and daily life, each with examples of local speech. Readers meet abbey-lubbers, gurt fields, gruff-holes dug for ore, and hackers chattering with cold. The glossary is a treasure for students of English dialect and Somerset history alike.
2564-wanderings-among-south-sea-savages-:
H. Wilfrid Walker, a Fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, published this travel record in 1909, with forty eight plates from photographs by himself and others. Most of the text comes straight from private letters he wrote in Dayak huts, Negrito camps, and deep tropical forest, in simple words meant for home.

Walker had no thought of a book when he wrote them, which gives the pages a fresh, unpolished feel. He describes customs, ornaments, hunts, and river journeys among South Sea peoples, in Borneo, and in the Philippines. The volume reads as a plain eyewitness tour of island worlds on the edge of great change.
27829-introduction-to-the-history-of-rel:
Crawford Howell Toy, late professor at Harvard, wrote this history of religions as volume four of the Handbooks on the History of Religions, edited by Morris Jastrow Jr. The Harvard University Press edition appeared in 1924, after a 1913 copyright.

Toy begins with the nature of religion, the soul, and early beliefs about death, then traces how religions developed alongside social organization. The volume treats religion as a human phenomenon across cultures, and it served students as a comparative survey before specialized studies took over the field. Later chapters treat the soul's origin, its future after death, and the dwelling-place of the surviving soul.
28529-an-impartial-narrative-of-the-most:
An Impartial Narrative of the Most Important Engagements was printed in Dublin in 1799, priced at one shilling and one penny. It collects accounts of battles between His Majesty's forces and the rebels during the Irish Rebellion of 1798. The editor gathered the material carefully from authentic letters.

He admits the battles are not in chronological order and make no great literary pretensions, but claims a more valuable quality: authenticity. Where a correspondent's report proved correct, he prints it in the correspondent's own language. The narrative forms a small portion of a larger work he hoped to complete, and it remains a contemporary witness to a year he calls an epoch in Irish history.
28627-incentives-to-the-study-of-the-anc:
Henry R. Schoolcraft's Incentives to the Study of the Ancient Period of American History is an address given before the New York Historical Society on its forty-second anniversary, 17 November 1846. Published at the society's request in 1847, it asks how far inquiry can narrow the mystery around the continent's early period. Schoolcraft frames the field rather than settling it.

He poses linked questions about peoples before the monarchies of Mexico and Peru, about Coxcox and Manco Capac, and about ties between Cuzco, Anahuac, Mexican pyramids, and Mississippi mounds. Physiology, languages, arts, monuments, and mental habits supply the clues. Readers get a call to study America's ancient past.
29077-byzantine-churches-in-constantinop:
Alexander Van Millingen, professor of history at Robert College in Constantinople, wrote this study of the city's Byzantine churches, assisted on architecture by Ramsay Traquair and others. Published by Macmillan with maps, plans, and illustrations, it treats churches that survived from the Byzantine capital into the modern city.

Van Millingen gives each church its history and its architecture: when it was built, how it changed under later rulers, and what its plan, masonry, and decoration show. A medieval map of Constantinople opens the book and helps readers place each building. Readers get a scholarly guide to a vanished capital's sacred buildings, useful both for historians and for travelers tracing Byzantium in stone.
29949-washington-s-masonic-correspondenc:
Julius F. Sachse, librarian of the Masonic Temple in Philadelphia, compiled Washington's Masonic Correspondence from the Washington papers in the Library of Congress, printed in Philadelphia in 1915. The work was done under the direction of the Committee on Library of the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania, with annotations, and its chairman was John Wanamaker. An edition of one thousand copies was printed, of which this copy is number 355.

A frontispiece reproduces the Masonic portrait of Brother General George Washington, a pastel from life by William Williams, painted in Philadelphia in September 1794 at the request of Alexandria Lodge Number 39. That lodge, warranted by the Grand Lodge of Pennsylvania in February 1783, is now Alexandria-Washington Lodge Number 22 of Virginia. The volume gathers Washington's Masonic letters with notes for readers of Masonic and early American history.
30609-the-message-and-the-man-some-essen:
J. Dodd Jackson delivers the fourteenth Hartley Lecture, The Message and the Man, on some essentials of effective preaching, in a second edition published in London in 1912. Jackson dedicates the book to his father, Rev. James Jackson, a Primitive Methodist preacher for fifty-five years and president of the Conference in 1897.

Its epigraph calls the preacher a workman needing not to be ashamed, rightly dividing the word of truth. Jackson notes it would be strange if, among annual lecture volumes, no book on preaching arrived, since preaching holds so large a place in worship and in the Redeemer's purposes. He treats content, quality, and the preacher's own life as essentials.
3165-rashi:
Maurice Liber writes the life of Rashi, the great medieval Jewish scholar of Troyes in France. Rashi, whose full name was Solomon ben Isaac, lived in the eleventh century and wrote the commentary on the Bible and the Talmud that students still study beside the text itself. His plain, exact notes shaped Jewish learning for centuries after him.

Liber follows Rashi from his school days to his standing as a master whose rulings guided a whole community. The book explains, in clear terms, what a commentary does and why this one endured. A quiet scholar's notes still anchor study centuries after they were written in Troyes.
32188-eikon-basilike-the-pourtracture-of:
Eikon Basilike, the Pourtracture of His Sacred Majestie in His Solitudes and Sufferings, was printed at London in 1649. Its title page adds that it holds a perfect copy of the king's prayers from the time of his sufferings. They were delivered to Dr. Juxon, Bishop of London, immediately before his death. The book presents the king's meditations from imprisonment and trial, framed as a royal portrait in words.

An explanation of the emblem opens the volume in Latin verse. It shows the palm pressed down yet rising, the rock repelling waves and wind, and the crown spurned for a crown of thorns. The mottoes set the tone: to do good and suffer evil is kingly. Readers get a famous seventeenth-century royalist text, part devotion, part apology, published in the year of the king's death.
33560-a-new-genus-of-pennsylvanian-fish-:
Joan Echols describes a previously unrecognized genus of coelacanth fish from Pennsylvanian rocks in Kansas. The specimens came from the Rock Lake shale near Garnett, in Anderson County, collected first in 1931 and 1932 and again from a second nearby locality in 1954 and 1955. Earlier workers had treated some of this material as the basis of two new species.

Echols re-examined all of the material, compared it with casts and specimens from other museums, and concluded that it represents a distinct genus, which she names and defines in systematic detail. The paper gives the anatomical evidence for that decision and places the new form among the lobe-finned fishes. It is a concise taxonomic study for readers of fossil fish.
34006-rustic-sounds-and-other-studies-in:
Sir Francis Darwin published this set of essays in London in 1917, with pictures. The title essay says sounds bring back childhood more keenly than sights, and Darwin wanders through seasons of his youth by ear: frozen puddles, spring, and summer lanes. Other essays treat Francis Galton, the movement of plants, and a lane in the Cotswolds.

Jane Austen, Stephen Hales, war music, the teaching of science, and dogs and dog lovers follow, with a study of his father, Sir George Darwin. Darwin writes as a naturalist with a literary bent. The book offers a gentle mix of memory, science, and reading.
37535-history-of-the-washington-national:
Frederick Harvey, secretary of the Washington National Monument Society, writes a History of the Washington National Monument and of the Society. The book was printed at Washington in 1902. Harvey sets the build craft aside as a theme for a split, expert account.

The history, he says, lies in the annals of Congress and the records of the Society. In the main it is the Society's own tale: its first formation, its charter by act of Congress, and its long, patriotic labors. Its aim was to raise a great monument to Washington at the seat of government. Its origin lies in the failure of Congress to keep a pledge made in 1783.
37753-notes-on-the-mammals-of-gogebic-an:
L R Dice and H B Sherman wrote Notes on the Mammals of Gogebic and Ontonagon Counties, Michigan, issued in February nineteen twenty-two. The paper is number one hundred and nine in a museum series from the University of Michigan. Field work ran through the summer of nineteen twenty.

The pair camped first in the Cisco Lake Region, then near Little Girl's Point, then by Lake Gogebic. The work was done for the state survey of geology and living things. Trappers gave records too, among them J E Fischer and Benjamin J Twombley. One trapper, J E Marshall, had worked the counties since eighteen eighty-four. The list notes each kind and its haunts.
39010-an-historical-view-of-the-philippi:
An Historical View of the Philippine Islands, volume one, is an English translation of a Spanish work by Martinez de Zuñiga, published at Manila in 1803. John Maver translated it, and the London edition shown here appeared in 1814. The title promises the islands' discovery, population, language, government, manners, customs, productions, and commerce. A new and accurate map of the islands accompanies the volumes.

The translator's introduction says the original was probably the only copy yet to reach England. Its information, he argues, fills a gap in English. It gives a correct view, down to a very late period, of the Spanish establishments in the Philippines, the Spanish colony most interesting to a British subject. A note in the copy adds the islands' commercial weight. They form the meeting-point of Europe, India, China, Spanish America, and the coasts of both the old world and the new.
39027-an-historical-view-of-the-philippi:
Martinez de Zuniga's Historical View of the Philippine Islands, published at Manila in 1803 and translated by John Maver, covers the islands' discovery, people, language, government, manners, productions, and commerce. This second volume, printed at London in 1814 with a new map, takes up the story in 1669. Chapter one follows Governor Manuel de Leon, who seized the goods of his interim predecessor, revived the China trade through envoys to Macao, and died suddenly at a wedding in 1677.

Succeeding chapters give Governor Vargas, whose good start rotted into avarice and quarrels between civil and church powers, and Governor Curuzalegui, whose prudence ended the dissensions before his death in 1689. The history proceeds governor by governor, year by year, in short annals. Zuniga was an Augustinian writing from inside the Spanish colonial church, and the translation made his account a standard English source on the Philippines.
39501-ladies-on-horseback-learning-park-:
Mrs Power O'Donoghue, writing as Nannie Lambert, wrote Ladies on Horseback, printed in London in 1881. The subtitle promises learning, park-riding, and hunting, with hints upon costume and numerous anecdotes. She gives the pages to her friend Alfred Watson, author of Sketches in the Hunting Field, to whom she owes much of her success as a writer. An introduction says the work is composed chiefly of papers on horses and their riders that appeared in the Illustrated Sporting and Dramatic News.

Those papers began, she tells, one day in the middle of February 1880. Thousands assembled on a nobleman's lawn near Dublin, ostensibly for hunting. In reality they came to gaze at a distinguished foreign lady lately come to those shores. Ladies on horseback hold a great attraction for her, she writes, for gentlemen riders are seen every hour, ladies seldom.
40105-baseball-joe-at-yale-or-pitching-f:
Lester Chadwick wrote this boys' baseball novel, published in New York in 1913 by Cupples and Leon. It is the third book in the Baseball Joe series, after Baseball Joe of the Silver Stars and Baseball Joe on the School Nine. The same author's College Sports series is listed at the front as well.

Joe leaves home for Yale, and the chapter list maps his first college season. He settles on campus, finds a new chum, and goes out for early practice. Trouble comes with a sneering rival, an unsigned letter, and a plot against him. One last game at home, a trip to face Cornell, and a shot at the college championship carry the action. Young fans of the diamond get a full season of school sport.
40387-studies-of-christianity-or-timely-:
James Martineau's Studies of Christianity, timely thoughts for religious thinkers, was published by the American Unitarian Association at Boston in 1858, edited by Alger. The contents list thirteen papers: types of Christianity, Christianity without priest and without ritual, the case against vicarious redemption, and mediatorial religion among them.

Five points of Christian faith, the creed and heresies of early Christianity, the creed and ethics of Christendom, and St Paul and his modern students fill the later pages. A preface tells Martineau's American history. The Association had reprinted his sermon on the state of theology as a tract in 1835, when he was a minister in Liverpool, and it won great praise. Since then his writings had widened his audience year by year, and this collection is printed as a favour to the reading public and a service to liberal Christianity.
43487-the-depot-for-prisoners-of-war-at-:
Thomas James Walker wrote a history of the depot for prisoners of war at Norman Cross in Huntingdonshire, issued in nineteen thirteen. Walker was a doctor and surgeon with posts in learned bodies. The depot held French prisoners from seventeen ninety-six to eighteen sixteen.

Early chapters tell why prison room was badly needed and why Norman Cross was chosen. Walker then describes the prison, its staff, and how new prisoners were logged on arrival. Prison life, work such as straw plait, escapes, and sickness all get chapters. Later pages cover the dead, the chapel, parole, marriages, and swaps of prisoners.
45268-the-native-races-of-the-pacific-st:
Hubert Howe Bancroft's Native Races closes with this fifth volume, Primitive History. A L Bancroft and Company published it at San Francisco in 1883, entered for copyright the year before. The set forms volume five of Bancroft's collected works. His preface notes that the volume went through the press over a year. Letters of encouragement had come from scholars of Europe and America, and learned societies had commended the work.

Bancroft owns that this first attempt broke a new field. The scope was very extensive, and the system and machinery for doing it untried. The subject, he adds, was not one of great popular interest. The earlier volumes treat the wild tribes, their manners, languages, and myths in turn. This last volume gives their primitive history: origins, migrations, and the oldest traditions.
54578-the-life-of-captain-sir-richard-f-:
The Life of Captain Sir Richard Burton, volume one, is the biography of the explorer by his wife, Isabel Burton. Chapman and Hall published it in London in 1893, in two volumes with portraits, illustrations, and maps. A picture shows Burton in his tent in Africa. Burton had died in 1890, and his widow made the book her consecration to him.

Her dedication calls him her earthly master, waiting for her on heaven's frontiers. She leaves the record of the life into which both their lives were fused. She wishes she could write as well as she can love, to do him the justice he deserves. Brighter pens, she says, will feel less and write better. Her foreword adds that she will call him simply Richard. The result is part biography, part devotion: the pilgrim to Mecca and translator of the Nights, told by the woman who shared his exile.
56002-studies-in-greek-scenery-legend-an:
Frazer wrote studies of Greek land, tale, and past that were picked from his larger works. Frazer is known for The Golden Bough and for his Greek guide books. He turned Pausanias into English with long notes and maps. His work deals with myth, rite, and the life of old Greece. These short pieces bring that work to a home reader.

Readers meet Greek hills, shrines, and towns as the old tales name them. Frazer sets tale next to place and asks what each tale grew from. His calm, clear prose suits slow study. The book suits those who love old Greece but lack his big sets.
5620-palaces-and-courts-of-the-expositio:
Juliet James wrote Palaces and Courts of the Exposition as a handbook to the architecture, sculpture, and mural paintings of San Francisco's Panama-Pacific exposition, with special reference to symbolism. Her foreword pictures a hill-crowned city by a silver sea near a Golden Gate, where water washes a land-locked bay and the shore forms an amphitheatre stretching three miles to western headlands.

The handbook guides visitors through palaces and courts, explaining what their sculpture and paintings mean. James writes for exposition visitors who want more than names. Readers get a vivid souvenir guide to the pastel city by the sea, useful as history and as art appreciation.
57801-early-days-in-fort-worth-much-of-w:
Early Days in Fort Worth is a memoir-history by Paddock, written just after 1900. Paddock says he was part of much of what he tells. The 2010 facsimile here reprints the rare first edition in three hundred copies. A plate shows Fort Worth's first bank building.

Paddock sets out to write a brief history of the town from its choice as a military post down to living memory. He pays close detail to the work of the men who laid the city's foundation. He feels they get too little credit from the uninformed. Their first thought, he writes, was always the upbuilding of the town. The book is a founder's tribute and a first-hand record of a Texas frontier post growing into a city.
57999-the-tragedies-of-seneca-translated:
The Tragedies of Seneca, turned into English verse by Frank Justus Miller, was printed by the University of Chicago Press in 1907. John Matthews Manly wrote a lead essay on the sway of Seneca over early English drama. A myth index stands at the back.

Miller adds side by side studies of the Greek and Roman plays on the same tales. A front plate shows a double bust of Seneca and Socrates, now in Berlin. Manly notes that the public stage was not the only place Seneca ruled in Shakespeare day. School and private plays spread his dark, bold manner wide. Students of drama get the full plays in verse, with the tools to weigh them against their Greek roots.
58535-the-gracious-designs-of-god-accomp:
The Gracious Designs of God is a church talk by Church at the Surrey Tabernacle. He spoke it on November twenty fourth, eighteen nineteen, his free day. A Thomas press of Southwark printed the talk in that same year. Its next name adds that foe hate worked out those kind plans in full. But God meant it unto good is the text line at its head.

The talk calls the church books a chart of the save plan for lost man. God love is its spring, Christ work its core, and the Ghost its hand. Light woes of a span work a vast weight of fame, it holds. A sworn God marks the path of his folk in love and wise care. Dark strokes and hard trials serve that great aim in the end.
58613-the-ph-nix-of-sodom-or-the-vere-st:
An anonymous pamphlet printed at London in 1813 exhibits the Vere Street coterie, a group of men arrested in a molly house raid of 1810. The title promises the gambols of the ancient lechers of Sodom and Gomorrah, improved with modern refinements. The writer opens by accounting for his acquaintance with the transactions disclosed. He owes that account, he says, to reader and himself alike.

The Vere Street men were pilloried and jailed amid public fury. The pamphlet mixes report, sermon, and scandal for the trade. Sold by J Cook and all booksellers, it fed a market for exposure literature. It is now read as evidence in the history of sexuality.
59237-excursions-in-the-county-of-cornwa:
Excursions in the County of Cornwall is a topographical guide by F W L Stockdale, author of Antiquities of Kent, published at London in 1824. Its title promises a concise historical and topographical delineation of the principal towns and villages of the county. Descriptions of the residences of the nobility and gentry go with it.

Remains of antiquity and every other interesting object of curiosity are included. The whole forms a complete guide for the traveller and tourist. Engravings show Truro from the square, Saint Germans church, and the font in Lostwithiel church. Stockdale drew on his own sketches and those of other hands for the plates. Such county excursion books were the guidebooks of their day, sold by subscription and by stationers. This one walks the reader through Cornwall parish by parish, church by church, and seat by seat, in the years after Waterloo.
59501-hieroglyfic-or-a-grammatical-intro:
Hieroglyfic, or A Grammatical Introduction to an Universal Hieroglyfic Language, by Jones, was printed at London in 1768 and sold by Dodsley and others. Its plan is vast: one system of signs and sounds for all mankind, built from English signs and voices, with definitions of the parts of speech in English, Welsh, Greek, and Latin.

The preface blames the corrupt state of modern tongues and the wrong road of dictionary makers. Jones offers his finds toward restoring the first universal language of mankind. Grand schemes for a perfect language filled the age, and few were grander or more earnest than this one.
60098-mr-rabbit-at-home-a-sequel-to-litt:
Joel Chandler Harris wrote Mr Rabbit at Home, a sequel to his queer country tales. Houghton, Mifflin and Company issued the book in Boston in eighteen hundred ninety five. Oliver Herford drew the pictures for the small volume. Harris was famed far and wide as the teller of Uncle Remus.

Buster John sounds the alarm that wakes Mr Rabbit in chapter one. Where the thunder lives and the jumping off place come next in turn. A magic ring and a cow with golden horns fill the mid tales. Brother Wolf plans two big dinners and fares ill at both. The Woog and the Weeze share one of the last strange tales. Uncle Rain and Brother Drouth close the queer country round. A snow white goat and a coal black sheep meet near the end.
60150-selling-latin-america-a-problem-in:
Selling Latin America, by William Aughinbaugh, came out at Boston in 1915 with many photographs. The sub-title calls it a problem in world salesmanship: what to sell and how to sell it. Aughinbaugh wrote for firms at home that sought trade to the south.

One chapter on foreign trade in general opens the book, and then the lands come one by one. Brazil, the Argentine, Uruguay, and Paraguay lead, then Chile, Bolivia, Peru, and Ecuador. Colombia, Venezuela, Central America, and Mexico follow, with Cuba and Haiti near the end. Later chapters treat methods of business, the salesman and his customer, and custom-houses. Trade marks, credit, packing, shipping, and health all get full chapters of their own.
62121-john-l-stoddard-s-lectures-vol-03-:
John L Stoddard's illustrated travel lectures fill ten volumes, of which the third, copyrighted in 1897, treats Japan in two lectures and China in a third. A picture titled Friends in Council opens the volume. Lecture one on Japan begins with Magellan. Nearly four hundred years have passed since he first sailed around the world, Stoddard says. Yet three years were once needed for the trip.

Stoddard performed his lectures with lantern slides to packed halls. The books preserve the talks with photographs on every page. Balch Brothers published the set at Boston in 1908. Japan and China, newly opened to Western tourists, drew his largest audiences.
64735-bear-ye-one-another-s-burdens-a-pl:
James Galloway Cowan, minister of Archbishop Tenison's Chapel in Regent Street, preached this plain sermon on the Lancashire distress in 1862. William Skeffington printed it in London that year. The title takes its text from Galatians, chapter six, verse two. Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ.

Cowan opens by sorting burdens into two kinds. Some burdens each man must bear for himself, such as those laid on him by sin: fear, remorse, and punishment. The charge for his gifts and chances likewise rests with him and God, and no stranger may meddle in it. Other burdens, the sermon goes on to argue, fall to be shared, and the distress in Lancashire gives the case.
65087-ben-the-trapper-or-the-mountain-de:
Ben, the Trapper; or, The Mountain Demon, a tale of the Black Hills by Major Lewis Carson, was published in New York by Beadle and Adams in 1875. The story opens in a deep defile among the Black Hills, where three men have made a camp. They are trappers of the North-west, a class the narrator calls a wonderful race.

The first chapter praises the trappers' hard, wandering life against cold, grizzly bears, snow-slides, and hostile foes, with only traps, a rifle, powder, and a blanket for wealth. Their creed, the book says, is the border creed: they should take who have the power, and they should keep who can. The chapters ahead promise a grizzly, the mountain devil, a buffalo hunt from a tree, and Indians. Beadle and Adams sold such tales as dime novels of the frontier.
70070-prose-remains-of-arthur-hugh-cloug:
Arthur Hugh Clough’s Prose Remains gathers his prose with a choice of his letters. His wife edited the book for Macmillan in London in eighteen hundred eighty eight. A memoir of the poet heads the thick volume of remains. Clough was born at Liverpool on January first, eighteen hundred nineteen.

His Welsh kin traced their line to Sir Richard Clough of old. That knight served Gresham at Antwerp in Tudor days. Letters run from Rugby school days in eighteen hundred twenty nine. Oxford, London, and America mark the next three long spans. A plea on Oxford cuts in the Irish famine stands here. Talks on Wordsworth’s verse and Dryden’s tongue join the set. A review weighs poems by Alexander Smith and Matthew Arnold. Notes on old faith lore close the book his wife built.
american-eloquence-volume-1-studies-in-a: Alexander Johnston opens his studies in American political history with volume one of American Eloquence, covering colonialism and the formation of the Constitution. Speeches by James Otis and others trace how American political language took shape before and during the founding. The volume gives students the key oratory of the early republic in context.
american-eloquence-volume-2-studies-in-a: Alexander Johnston continues American Eloquence in volume two, where the anti-slavery struggle dominates the political stage. Speeches by Rufus King, William Pinkney, and Wendell Phillips show the moral and legal arguments over slavery gathering force. The collection lets readers hear the debate in the voices that shaped it, and feel how urgent the question had become.
american-eloquence-volume-3-studies-in-a: Alexander Johnston devotes volume three of American Eloquence to secession, including the Lincoln-Douglas debate and speeches by William Seward. The oratory traces the road from compromise to crisis, as North and South argued over union, slavery, and the Constitution. It is a vivid record of American politics at its most fateful hour.
american-eloquence-volume-4-studies-in-a: Alexander Johnston closes American Eloquence with volume four, on civil war and reconstruction, free trade and protection, and finance and civil service reform. The speeches follow the nation through war, rebuilding, and the economic questions of the Gilded Age. Together the four volumes form a full course in American political speech.
anti-achitophel-1682-three-verse-replies: Harold Whitmore Jones gathers Anti-Achitophel of 1682, three verse replies to Dryden's Absalom and Achitophel, in scholars' facsimiles and reprints from the British Museum and Florida libraries. The replies answer Dryden's satire in kind, defending the Whig cause in verse. Jones's edition preserves a sharp exchange of Restoration politics. The verse replies sting as sharp as Dryden's own.
britannica-1911-ashi: ʾAshi (352–427) was a Jewish amora, a Talmudic sage. He was the first editor of the Talmud. Babylon was his birthplace. He headed the Sura Academy there. At Sura he began the Babylonian Talmud. Thirty years of his life went into it. He left the work incomplete at death. His disciple Rabina finished it afterwards. That completion came just before 500 A.D. The entry is very short. It points readers to the Talmud article for the work itself and its long editorial history.
britannica-1911-bauchi:
Bauchi is a province in the highlands of Northern Nigeria, in West Africa under British rule, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Its area is about 21,000 square miles. The land rises from 1000 feet in the north-east to 6000 feet in the south-west. A belt of ranges and rich plateaus crosses it, and the south holds dead volcanic craters.

High ground shapes the province's fame. The Assab or Kibyen plateau and the Sura country stand from 3000 to over 4000 feet up. Their soil is rich, pure water is plentiful, and the air is keen and bracing, much like that of the Transvaal. These plateaus form the main watershed of Northern Nigeria. The Gongola flows from Sura to the Benue; other streams run to Lake Chad, the Kaduna, and the Benue. Winter cold on the heights can reach freezing point.
britannica-1911-chukchi:
The Chukchi are a people of the far north east of Siberia. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets them on the shores of the Arctic Ocean and Bering Sea. Their land spans some 300,000 square miles. Yet their numbers were put at only a few thousand. They live in small groups along the coast. Some roam inland as far as the Anadyr basin. A voyage of 1878 gave the first close study of them.

The entry dwells on their build and looks. It calls them tall and lean, with broad flat faces and high cheek bones. Their hair is coarse, straight, and black. Some writers place them as a link between the peoples of Asia and America. Old wars with the first folk of the coast are noted. So is mixing with Koryak and Eskimo groups near Bering Strait. The account shows the era's habit of sorting peoples by skull shape.
britannica-1911-delhi:
Delhi is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article on the ancient capital of the Mogul empire in India. The modern city gives its name to a district and division of British India. It stands very nearly due north of Cape Comorin, on a line with the old cities of Cairo and Canton. The city lies in the south east corner of the Punjab.

Delhi sits on the right bank of the river Jumna, the entry notes. Lahore stays the official capital of the Punjab, but Delhi is more famous in history. It is now more important as a trading and railway centre too. Remains of earlier cities are scattered round it over a wide area. Modern Delhi dates only from the middle of the seventeenth century, when Shah Jahan rebuilt it on its present site.
britannica-1911-delphi:
Delphi is the subject of a place entry in the 1911 Britannica. Delphi was a town in old Greece in Phocis. It was famed as the seat of the shrine of Apollo. Its oracle was the most prized in the Greek world. The site lay inland from the Gulf of Corinth. Steep cliffs of Mount Parnassus shut it in on the north. A stream and a famed spring ran through the glen.

A large cave on the mount gave the folk a refuge. Greeks fled there when Persia invaded their land. A French backed dig cleared the site from 1892. A modern village on the site was bought and moved. The old precinct walls can now be traced in full. A paved Sacred Way winds up the hill. Shrines and gift bases line that road on both sides. Old texts help name the halls found in the dig.
britannica-1911-kashi:
Kashi, or Kasi, was once the Persian word for all glazed and enamelled pottery. It is now the set term for certain kinds of enamelled tile work, counting brick work and tile mosaic. Such work was made in Persia and parts of Muslim India, chiefly in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The word grows from a Semitic root for glass, kas. The name kashi may come at once from Kashan, a Persian town famed for its faïence, though that town may itself take its name from the old craft practised there. The art of glazing earthenware has come down in Persia in a near unbroken line from the great days of Chaldaea and Assyria. The name kas carries the craft back to the glass work for which Sidon was famed fifteen centuries before Christ.
britannica-1911-marathi:
Marathi, a tongue of west and mid India, is mapped in a long speech entry in the 1911 Britannica. Speakers in nineteen oh one came to more than eighteen million. That count matched the folk of Spain at the time. The tongue fills a rough triangle of one hundred thousand square miles. Poona speech sets the norm for the whole tongue. Settlers carry it far past its home tract as well.

Old roots of the tongue lie in the Outer Band of Aryan speech, the text says. Folk from the north plain pushed south past the Vindhya hills in time. There they met Dravidian tongue groups of the south. Their speech won out and was passed to the folk of the tract. Forms near Gujarat show a mix from that long path south.
britannica-1911-sibawaihi:
Sibawaihi, who lived from about 753 to 793, was a grammarian of Arabic. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica calls his grammar the first full system. Born a Persian freedman, he left no record of his youth. At thirty-two he went to Basra to study under Khalil.

A public clash with a rival scholar drove him from Baghdad. He went home to Persia and died near the age of forty. His great work is known to Arabs simply as The Book. It is the earliest full account of Arabic grammar ever made. Arabs rank it as the most perfect of its kind. Rich quotes from the Koran and the poets fill its pages. French and German editions carried it to the West in the 1800s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-angelo-secchi:
Angelo Secchi, astronomer, was born at Reggio in Italy in 1818 and died in 1878. Son of a joiner, he studied in his town's Jesuit school and entered the order at Rome in 1833, at sixteen. After studies at the Roman College, his talent made him tutor of mathematics and physics at Rome in 1839 and professor of physics at Loreto in 1841. He studied theology from 1844 and was ordained priest in 1847.

The 1848 revolution drove him from Rome through Paris and Stonyhurst to Georgetown near Washington, where he finished his doctorate and taught physics. Returning in 1849, he directed the Roman College observatory from 1850, and by 1852 had an observatory on Saint Ignatius church. His study was the sun. His 1860 eclipse expedition to Spain first proved by photographs that the corona and prominences were solar features. From 1863 he worked on some 4,000 stellar spectra, reducing all fixed stars to a few spectral types, the five Secchi types.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antonio-magli:
Florentine scholar and librarian Antonio Magliabechi, born in 1633 and dead there in 1714, rose from a goldsmith's bench to the centre of Italian letters. Apprenticed to a goldsmith, he worked at the trade until forty, buying books from small means and reading them after dark. Michele Ermini, librarian to Cardinal de' Medici, saw his ability and taught him Latin, Greek, and Hebrew. His memory astonished visitors, and he gathered unusually wide learning.

In 1673 he became librarian for Grand Duke Cosimo III of Tuscany, the ambition of his life, and scholars from every nation sought his company and letters. He answered questions freely and so became the unacknowledged helper behind many works. Strangers stared at him as a marvel, since he seemed to know every volume in the library, and even the page and paragraph where a passage stood. Private habits and oddities fill out the portrait.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ausonio-franc:
Ausonio Franchi was the pen name of Cristoforo Bonavino, an Italian philosopher born at Pegli near Genoa in 1821, who died there in 1895. He entered the priesthood and directed a secondary school at Genoa, but French positivism and German criticism filled him with doubt. A struggle followed, described in his book on the philosophy of the Italian schools. Amid the revolution of 1848, led by political and philosophical passion, he left priestly habit and office in 1849.

His new name, Ausonio Franchi, means free Italian, and it marked his break with his past. From then he fought the dogmatic authority of Church and the despotic authority of State, joining Kant's phenomenalism to Comte's positivism in a relativism and agnosticism. For him, religious truth and reason, Catholicism and liberty, could not be reconciled, and he chose freedom. In 1854 he founded the weekly Ragione, and later taught the history of philosophy at Pavia and Milan.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-campo-santo-d:
The Campo Santo de' Tedeschi, the Holy Field of the Germans, is a cemetery, church, and hospice for Germans. It stands on the south side of Saint Peter's in Rome, over part of Nero's Circus Vaticanus, where many Christians died by Nero's order. After Constantine built his basilica over the apostles' graves, the faithful sought burial nearby, chiefly on the south side, in the earth that filled the circus. Since the fifteenth century its soil has been held as sacred earth from Jerusalem.

In 796 Charlemagne, with Pope Leo III's leave, founded a hospice there for pilgrims of his empire. It had a church of the Saviour and a graveyard for his subjects who died in Rome. The house, called the Schola Francorum, fell into decay during the Avignon papacy and the Schism. It revived after the popes returned, when the German colony at Rome renewed Charlemagne's foundation under Martin V.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-carlo-odescal:
Carlo Odescalchi was a cardinal, prince, archbishop, and Jesuit born at Rome in March 1786. He died at Modena in August 1841. His father, Duke of Sirmium and Prince of the Roman Empire, schooled him personally. The boy soon showed a religious vocation. Ordained a priest, he said his first Mass on 1 January 1809. He won the trust of many, including a young cleric who became Pius IX and Gioacchino Pecci, the future Leo XIII, whom he ordained.

He attended Pius VII through the perils before the pope's captivity. He then rose swiftly with two special missions to Vienna. The cardinalate came in 1823, with the Archbishopric of Ferrara, which he resigned in 1826. As Bishop of Sabina he headed congregations and sat in the conclaves that chose Leo XII, Pius VIII, and Gregory XVI. A cell stood ready at Sant'Andrea after he resolved to join the restored Society of Jesus in 1814.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-costanzo-gius:
Costanzo Giuseppe Beschi, an Italian Jesuit born at Castiglione in 1680, spent nearly forty years in India's Madura mission. Arriving in 1710, he mastered Tamil grammar within five years and then studied the whole field of Tamil letters for twenty more, until native scholars bowed to him as their master.

Grammars of high and low Tamil, several dictionaries, doctrinal books for catechists, and tracts against Danish Lutheran rivals flowed from his pen. Poetry made him famous: the Tembavani, an epic of Saint Joseph in thirty-six cantos and 3,615 stanzas, stands beside a satire on native gurus that still entertains Tamil readers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filippo-scann:
Filippo Scannabecchi was a Bolognese painter born about 1360 and dead about 1410. Almost nothing is known of his life, except that he made his will in 1410. His father Dalmasio trained him, and he was among the earliest painters of Bologna. He was one of the first to give beauty to the Madonna and Child's features.

Malvasia praised his work highly, saying no great Bolognese family lacked an example of it. Modern critics find no surviving work that seems to deserve such praise. He is called Lippo dalle Madonne because he usually painted the Madonna. The name Muratori belongs to another Scannabecchi and should not be applied to him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francesco-zan:
Francesco Zantedeschi, born in 1797 and dead at Padua on 29 March 1873, was a priest and physicist of tireless output, with 325 memoirs and communications to his name. He taught physics and philosophy at the Liceo of Venice, then held the chair of physics at Padua University until failing sight forced his resignation in 1853. His work touched electricity, magnetism, and light at a time when those fields were still taking shape.

In 1829 and 1830 he published papers on electric currents produced in closed circuits by moving a magnet near and away, anticipating Faraday's classic experiments of 1831. Studying the solar spectrum, he was among the first to note how the atmosphere absorbs red, yellow, and green rays. In 1838 he thought he saw ultra-violet light act magnetically on steel needles, an effect never confirmed. It was yet a guess at the link between light and magnetism that Maxwell would formalise in 1867.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giacomo-gaeta:
Giacomo Gaetani Stefaneschi was a cardinal-deacon born at Rome about 1270, who died at Avignon in 1343. Son of the senator Pietro Stefaneschi, he studied at Paris. He became a canon of St. Peter's, and was made cardinal-deacon by Boniface VIII in 1295. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents him chiefly as a writer, never ordained a priest, whose verse life of Celestine V remains its earliest biography.

His Opus Metricum, in dactylic hexameter, tells of Celestine's election, reign, and abdication. It goes on to his later life, canonization, and miracles, in three parts joined in 1319. The poem holds great historical value but little literary grace, and at times turns clumsy. He also wrote on the first Roman Jubilee of 1300, on the ceremonies of the Roman court, on St. George, and on a miracle of the Virgin at Avignon.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-anto:
Giovanni Antonio Bianchi was a Franciscan theologian born at Lucca in 1686, who died at Rome in 1768. He entered the Franciscan Order at seventeen, taught philosophy and theology for years, and served once as provincial of the Roman province. Benedict XIV made him consultor of the Holy Office. A Catholic Encyclopedia article marvels at a memory so wide that scholars visited his cell as a prodigy.

His great work defended papal rights against the Neapolitan lawyer Pietro Giannone, in six volumes published at Rome between 1745 and 1751. Its first part upheld the pope's indirect power over temporal rulers, while the rest defended his rule over the Church's outward laws and government. In 1753 he also defended the lawfulness of modern theater, within limits, against the Dominican Concina, and he wrote poetry and tragedy besides.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-girolamo-tira:
Girolamo Tiraboschi was an Italian scholar born in the region of Bergamo in 1731, who died on 3 June 1794. He entered the Society of Jesus young, taught rhetoric and belles-lettres at the Brera in Milan, and was called by Duke Francesco III of Modena to direct the Biblioteca Estense. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows a librarian who enriched his library with books, manuscripts, and catalogues.

His chief work, the monumental Storia della letteratura italiana, runs from Etruscan times down to 1700. It covers belles-lettres, philosophy, history, the fine arts, medicine, and jurisprudence. Written in a clear and attractive style, it appeared between 1772 and 1782, then again at Modena between 1787 and 1794 with additions. His minor writings include the Biblioteca Modenese, an account of writers born in Modena, and a life of Fulvio Testi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giuseppe-marc:
Giuseppe Marchi was an archaeologist born at Tolmezzo near Udine on 22 February 1795, who died at Rome on 10 February 1860. He entered the Society of Jesus at Rome in 1814, taught humanities in several colleges, and became professor of rhetoric at the Roman College until 1842. A Catholic Encyclopedia article follows the master who opened the catacombs to study.

Made prefect of the Kircher Museum in 1838, he turned to Christian antiquities hoping to restore Christian art. In 1840 he announced a great publication of its monuments. In 1842 Gregory XVI made him Conservator of the sacred cemeteries of Rome. His young companion Giovanni Battista De Rossi learned from him, and in 1844 Marchi published the first volume of his Monumenti on the construction of the catacombs, especially Saint Agnes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-horacio-caroc:
Horacio Carochi was a Jesuit linguist, born at Florence about 1586 and dead in Mexico in 1666. He joined the Society of Jesus, then went to Mexico before finishing philosophy, and there studied native languages, above all Nahuatl and Otomi, which he fully mastered. He became secretary of the province.

His works include an Arte of the Mexican language with all its adverbs, printed at Mexico in 1645, a copious Mexican vocabulary, an Otomi grammar, an Otomi vocabulary, and sermons in Mexican. Only the first named work reached print. It remains a rare book and a highly valued contribution to Mexican linguistics, and his letters to Bishop Palafox of Puebla also deserve mention.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-james-laderch:
Italian Oratorian and church historian James Laderchi was born about 1678 at Faenza near Ravenna. He died at Rome on 25 April 1738. He is chiefly known for continuing the Annals of Baronius and Raynaldus. He carried them from 1566 down to 1571. His work, though useful, was not critical enough. It was also burdened with many unimportant documents. It appeared at Rome from 1728 to 1737.

In the latest Baronius edition it runs from volume 35 to volume 37. Laderchi also wrote several other historical works. Two of them drew him into heated literary quarrels. His large Life of St Peter Damian, published at Rome in 1702, was mercilessly but excessively criticized in an anonymous Paris dialogue of 1705. His edition of the Acts of St Crescentius' martyrdom drew similar fire. The entry presents a diligent annalist whose thoroughness outran his judgment.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-respi:
Lorenzo Respighi was an Italian astronomer, born at Cortemaggiore in 1824 and dead at Rome in 1889. Trained in mathematics and natural philosophy at Parma and Bologna, he took his degree in 1845 and rose to direct the Bologna observatory.

At Bologna from 1855 to 1864 he found three comets and published work in meteorology and astronomy. Refusing an oath to Victor Emmanuel's dynasty in 1865 cost him his chair, and he moved to Rome's Capitol observatory, which he directed from 1866. There he studied the lunar crater Linnaeus, star twinkling, and the sun's edge by spectrum light, dodging a second oath row in 1871.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-marcello-malp:
Marcello Malpighi was the founder of comparative physiology, born at Crevalcore in 1628 and dead at Rome in 1694. His birth year saw Harvey's book on blood circulation, which Malpighi would complete by tracing the capillaries. Raised on his father's farm, he entered Bologna University about seventeen, but his father, mother, and grandmother died in his last undergraduate year.

As eldest child he left to settle family affairs, returning after two years to medicine, where Professor Massari spotted him. He took his doctorate in medicine and philosophy in 1653 and married Massari's sister Francesca the next year. Microscope work named the rete Malpighi in skin, bodies in spleen and kidney, and the chick's growth in the egg, while plant vessels led to his Anatome plantarum of 1675. At sixty-four, Pope Innocent XII, his friend, called him to Rome as papal physician, where he died of apoplexy.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-muzio-vitelle:
Muzio Vitelleschi, born at Rome on 2 December 1563, was the sixth general of the Society of Jesus. He died there on 9 February 1645, elected on 15 November 1615 by the seventh general congregation. Of a distinguished family with brilliant prospects, he entered the Society in 1583 and taught as a professor. He became rector of the English College in 1593.

Later provincial for Rome and Naples and assistant to the general for Italy, he led the order through a period of high prosperity. He extended missions to Tibet, Tonking and the Maranon and raised the English mission to an independent province. His only serious troubles came in France, where Richelieu's pressure led him to forbid subordinates to speak or write of papal supremacy. In 1617 and 1619 he regulated the doctrine of probabilism by general letters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolo-de-tud:
Sicilian canon lawyer Nicolo de' Tudeschi, called Panormitanus, shaped late medieval church law from Sicily to the Council of Basel. Born at Catania in 1386, he joined the Benedictines, took a doctorate at Bologna in 1411, and taught canon law at Parma, Siena, and Bologna.

Made abbot near Messina and then archbishop of Palermo in 1435, he served Alfonso of Sicily and later backed the antipope Felix V, who made him cardinal. His commentaries on the Decretals, the Sext, and the Clementines earned him the name Light of Canon Law, and he died in 1445.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pneumatomachi:
The Pneumatomachi, or Combators against the Spirit, were a fourth-century sect that denied the divinity of the Holy Ghost. They are also called Macedonians after their founder Macedonius. He was intruded into the see of Constantinople by the Arians in 342 and enthroned by the emperor Constantius.

Macedonius persecuted Novatians and Catholics alike for holding the Son consubstantial with the Father. He expelled, imprisoned, and even tortured those who refused his communion. His disgrace followed his unauthorised disinterment of Constantine's body and the bloodshed he caused. He was deposed in 360 and died about 364, having, it is thought, framed his denial of the Spirit in his last years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-prefecture-ap:
The Capuchins received this Belgian Congo prefecture, cut on 7 April 1911 from the Belgian Congo's vicariate. Its bounds run west and north along the Ubanghi river, from 1° 30' north latitude to Yakoma, where the Mbomu meets the Uelle. East runs a line from that point toward the Itimbri, or Rubi, and Congo junction, as far as Abumombasi village's south limits.

South runs the parallel through Abumombasi, then the Ubanghi-Congo and Ubanghi-Ngiri watersheds, to 1° 30' north latitude, and thence to the Ubanghi. On 11 July 1911 R. P. Fulgence de Gérard-Montes took the first prefect apostolic's post.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-somaschi:
The Somaschi were a congregation of regular clerics devoted to charity, founded in the sixteenth century by St. Jerome Emiliani with its mother-house at Somasca near Venice. This entry gives the order's latest statistics rather than its full history, directing readers to the article on its founder for the story of its growth.

Across three provinces, Rome, Lombardy, and Liguria, the congregation counted sixteen houses and about 180 members, split between priests, clerics, and lay brothers. At Rome it ran three houses, including the general's residence and a novitiate, a parish with an orphanage. And a home for blind boys, while elsewhere it managed colleges, orphanages. And parishes, a compact picture of a working charitable order.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-maria-:
Thomas Maria Mamachi, Dominican theologian and historian, was born at Chios in 1713 and died at Corneto, Italy, in 1792. He entered the convent at Chios at sixteen, moved to Florence and Rome, and taught physics at the Sapienza in 1740 and philosophy at the Propaganda in 1743. Contact with Orsi, Divelli and Concina sharpened his studies, and he worked with Orsi on papal power over councils.

Benedict XIV named him a consultor of the Congregation of the Index, master of theology, and prefect of the Casanatensian Library. That office dragged him into the Jansenist-Jesuit quarrels, where his even-handedness pleased neither side. He also directed Rome's ecclesiastical journal from 1742 to 1785 and hosted a learned circle at his home.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ubanghi:
Ubangi was a vicariate apostolic in French Equatorial Africa, set up on 14 October 1890 from the older vicariate of French Congo. A vicariate apostolic is a mission district led by a bishop acting for the pope. It covered some 386,000 square miles, bounded by the Congo and Ubangi rivers to the south and east. To the north lay the new prefecture of Ubangi-Chari, and to the west the vicariates of Loango, Gabon, and Cameroon. Its peoples included the Bateke, Bavanziri, and Bondjo.

French officials such as de Chavannes and de Dolisie aided the mission's growth. Bishop Augouard's first attempt at Brazzaville in 1883 had failed, after harsh treatment of the natives by outsiders. The account lists later stations, priests, and schools, and notes the transfer of the Linzolo mission from Loango in 1911. It offers a compact administrative portrait of a vast mission territory in its first two decades.
doe-osti-2589383-microstructure-based-un:
Argonne National Laboratory report ANL-AMMT-023 studies how 3D-printed stainless steel holds up under heat and load. Authors Xuan Zhang, Yiren Chen, Lin Gao, and co-authors focus on type 316H steel made by laser powder bed fusion, a printing method that melts metal powder layer by layer. Parts from this process have a different inner structure than rolled steel, and that shapes how they deform.

Samples were aged at high temperature, some for as long as 10,000 hours, then pulled, crept, and cycled in tension and fatigue tests. Test temperatures matched aging temperatures of 550, 650, and 750 degrees Celsius. Curves compare printed samples with rolled steel of the same grade. The work supports judging whether printed 316H parts can serve in hot reactor systems, where slow stretching over years is a key failure path.
doe-osti-2589891-establishing-defect-pro:
University of Florida final report on award DE-SC0019014, led by Assel Aitkaliyeva, links controlled damage in atom-thin materials to changes in their behavior. Two-dimensional nanomaterials are sheets one or few atoms thick. The guiding bet was that ion beams could set defect levels on purpose, tuning light, electronic, and structural traits instead of merely degrading them.

Studies tracked how strain grows with ion dose and how stacked bilayer sheets settle into ordered moire patterns, the interference patterns of two grids. Sound wave tests tied stiffness to defect levels, measuring a Young's modulus of 247 gigapascals, plus or minus 9, in line with theory. Results give device makers a dial: dose the sheet, predict the property shift, and design around it.
doe-osti-3017708-development-of-next-gen:
Ashley Gomez of Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory wrote this progress report, LLNL-TR-2013988, in February 2026. It is the sixth-month report to her PhD committee, dated November 2025. The project develops next-generation battery anodes by direct ink writing, a printing method that lays down patterned material layer by layer. The anodes are hierarchical hybrids of copper and silicon, meant to beat plain graphite.

Graphite is running out of headroom as an anode material, while silicon stores far more but swells and cracks. The report tracks printed copper-silicon samples at several silicon loadings. A loading near 15 weight percent silicon looks like the maximum threshold before samples turn brittle. The 15 percent sample was far weaker than its lower-silicon counterparts. Pure silicon samples, in both micron and nano sizes, were still pending at report time. The committee record shows a doctoral project mid-flight, with its key trade-off already visible.
doe-osti-3019570-enhanced-design-of-radi:
Bibo Zhong and Joshua E Daw of Idaho National Laboratory redesigned sensors that listen for cracks in INL/RPT-25-89103, November 2025. Acoustic emission sensors catch the high-frequency stress waves that defects release as they form. In reactors, they watch vessels, piping, and containment for damage. The catch is environment: radiation and high temperature kill sensors. The enhanced design therefore targets radiation tolerance and heat together. A horn-shaped transition part amplifies the signals before electronics see them.

Three horn geometries, labeled designs A, B, and C, competed in ABAQUS simulations. A 200 kilohertz tone burst applied to each horn's base simulated emission energy. That frequency was chosen from prior work. Amplification performance decided the winner. For materials testing reactors, where these sensors monitor fuels under irradiation in real time, sensitivity is the difference between catching a crack and reading about it later. The report freezes the design analysis behind the choice.
doe-osti-3031192-supplement-analysis-for:
James R. Jackson and Joseph Rivers of the Energy Department Office of Nuclear Energy wrote this supplement analysis, PNNL-38351, dated April 2026. The department wants to ship the High Burnup Research Cask from the North Anna site to Idaho National Laboratory. The TN-32B cask holds high burnup spent fuel from a study program. Labs in Idaho can open and test such fuel; the shipping site cannot. The analysis checks the move against earlier environmental reviews.

At the Idaho site, the cask would ride the site rail system to the Idaho Nuclear Technology and Engineering Center. One option uses a rail spur about 3.5 miles north that may need upgrades and a cleared pad for crane work. After unloading, the cask goes to the CPP-2707 storage pad, and later steps move it inside the fence for exams.
doe-osti-3362580-data-quality-assessment:
Casey Quinn, Paden Rumsey, and Kang-Ching Chu of Idaho National Laboratory audit a driving dataset in report INL/RPT-25-85953, dated December 2024. In October 2024 the lab received Optiwatt telematics on about 10,000 electric vehicles, from 9 makes and 18 models built from 2012 to 2024, though over 9,500 were Teslas. The records hold more than six million trips and three million charging events, from June 2023 to August 2024 in California and the eastern states.

Quality checks found cracks. A screening tool flagged 1,132 records that pointed to IDs missing from the lookup tables, all in customer and user files. Thirty-six trips began and ended at zero battery charge, and about 500 drives ended at zero from a higher start. Some 800 charging records claimed no power while still logging energy delivered.
doe-osti-3363717-energy-to-communities-e:
The Energy to Communities program, funded by DOE and managed by the National Laboratory of the Rockies with Argonne, Lawrence Berkeley, Oak Ridge, and Pacific Northwest laboratories, publishes its 2025 annual highlights. The program links local governments, Tribes, utilities, and community organizations with laboratory experts for tailored energy analysis.

In 2025 it served representatives from 166 communities, and since launching in 2023 it has supported more than 500 participants. Three offerings structure the help: Expert Match for targeted questions, Peer-Learning Cohorts that gather up to 15 participants for six months, and In-Depth Partnerships for sustained work. Quoted participants praise the in-person exchanges most.
doe-osti-3403165-update-on-radiochemical:
Report ORNL/TM-2026/4712 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, dated July 2026, updates lab checks of high burnup fuel from commercial reactors. Jason M. Harp, Matthew M. Jones, Tamara J. Keever, Micah Best, and Nathan A. Capps wrote the update. The fuel came from the Byron plant cycles covered in the study.

Lab staff measured the fuel chemistry after irradiation and compared it with model results. The VERA code simulated each Byron cycle, with control rod moves included. Close matches build trust in models of fuel behavior during use and after removal. The results also help staff read non-destructive burnup checks with more care.
doe-osti-3520834-mass-spectrometry-chara:
Report ORNL/SPR-2025/4088 from Oak Ridge National Laboratory, dated August 2025, examines high fluence baffle-former bolts pulled from a Westinghouse pressurized water reactor. Timothy G. Lach, Gabriel Parker, Xiao-Ying Yu, and Xiang Chen wrote the study. These bolts hold core internals under stress and heavy neutron dose.

Surface spectra came from time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry. A 30 keV bismuth ion beam probed the bolt surfaces. An oxygen sputter beam cleaned surfaces at set current during runs. Chemical maps show how years of reactor service changed the bolt metal. Life extension teams learn which bolt changes signal real degradation.
nasa-tm-19660012906-methods-of-confusion:
James A Duke at Ames Research Center studied how people go wrong when they match patterns. Experiments on pattern perception often damage a pattern to make it harder to name. The ways of damaging it have varied almost as much as the experiments, Duke notes. His question is whether those methods can be matched to each other in effect, so results can be compared fairly.

Patterns were built by filling cells in a grid at random. Damage then added cells, moved them, or changed their state. Each method confuses the eye in its own way. Duke's task sorts out those confusions. Such work served display design, where crews have to read symbols quickly and correctly under strain.
nasa-tm-19660020881-apollo-saturn-1b-fli:
Kennedy Space Center issued this flight safety plan on June 1, 1966, for Apollo Saturn IB vehicle AS-203. Approvals came from Arthur H Moore of the technical staff, from G M Preston of launch operations, and from Rocco A Petrone, Apollo program manager at the center. The plan runs to fourteen pages, with a list of effective pages at its head.

Flight safety covers the people and property around a launch. Requirements, restrictions, and safety instrumentation are its core, per the catalog note. AS-203 flew an uncrewed Apollo test soon after this plan. A signed plan fixed the rules before the vehicle reached the pad, so every team worked from the same page.
nasa-tm-19670008502-lubrication-and-wear:
Robert L. Johnson and Donald H. Buckley, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a lubrication conference in London, England, in September 1967. It lays out the fundamentals of friction, lubrication, and wear for machinery that must work in a high vacuum, as spacecraft mechanisms do.

Most vacuum problems, the authors explain, come from low pressure and the lack of oxygen. Protective oxide films cannot be maintained, lubricants evaporate, and heat escapes poorly. They show how the adhesion concept of friction ties together cleavage and sliding studies. Crystal structure matters greatly: metals and alloys with a hexagonal structure near the ideal stacking ratio show useful friction and wear behavior. Sliding surfaces bond through diffusion, chemical action, or mechanical locking, and material transfer follows from those bonds.
nasa-tm-19670030324-application-of-a-met:
G. R. Halford and S. S. Manson, of NASA's Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, prepared this paper for a national metal congress in Cleveland, Ohio, in October 1967. It applies a method for estimating how materials behave under low cycle fatigue at high temperature. Low cycle fatigue is the slow cracking from repeated heating, cooling, and straining. It afflicts machines like gas turbines and nuclear reactors.

The method estimates strain fatigue life in the creep range from two simpler kinds of data: tensile properties and stress-rupture properties. It builds on an equation of universal slopes developed for room-temperature fatigue, plus a linear damage analysis combining fatigue and rupture. The authors compare their estimates against a large body of laboratory fatigue data. Materials covered include nickel-base alloys, high and low alloy steels, stainless steels, and aluminum alloys, tested across wide ranges of temperature and cycling rate.
palaces-and-courts-of-the-exposition-a-h:
Juliet James wrote Palaces and Courts of the Exposition as a handbook. It covers the fair's architecture, sculpture, and mural paintings. Special reference to their symbolism guides the whole. The fair was San Francisco's Panama-Pacific Exposition of 1915. It celebrated the Panama Canal's completion. James explains what the pastel palaces meant.

Her foreword, The Pastel City by the Sea, sets the scene. A hill-crowned city stands by a silver sea, near a Golden Gate. Three years before, the fairground was marsh and lagoon. Then a phantom flotilla of caravels arrived. Energy, Enterprise, and Youth stood at their prows. Venus rode in front, holding the golden ball of opportunity. The handbook decodes the city those spirits built.
podcast-dannyjones-rK-mynKHtHI:
Max Lebow joins Danny Jones to claim that China runs its own MK-Ultra and that 5G towers are part of the plan. The episode title asks why China wants the towers spread so wide. Lebow brings the claim in full.

Lebow argues the towers and the waves they send could be used to sway minds at scale. He links the claim to the old US mind control tests he says set the mold. Jones asks what proof can be put on the table. Listeners get a dark tech claim whole. The library holds the talk as an archive record, without a verdict.
profiles-from-china-sketches-in-free-ver:
Eunice Tietjens published sketches in free verse from the Chinese interior in 1917, dedicating the book to her mother. Short poems picture people and things seen far from the coast, in towns, temples, shops, and fields.

The contents move from cormorants, a scholar, and a story teller to a feast, a beggar, a city wall, and Chinese New Year. A second group, Echoes, adds the Festival of the Dragon Boats and a lament of Scarlet Cloud. Readers get quick, sharp portraits of daily life and belief in a changing China, drawn from travel far inland.
rashi: Rashi, by Maurice Liber, is shown here by its Project Gutenberg header alone. The header prints the book's title and author. It prints the cautions that copyright laws are changing all over the world. It pleads with readers to keep the file on their own disks for future readers. It prints the Literary Archive Foundation's donation appeals. The states then solicited are listed. The biography itself begins beyond these pages.
tanakh-jps-1917-malachi:
Malachi is the last of the short prophetic books, here in the Jewish Publication Society translation dated 1917. It is styled the burden of God's word to Israel by the hand of Malachi.

God states his love for Jacob, set against his hate for Esau, whose hills were left waste to jackals. The priests answer back with doubts at each charge, a back-and-forth that fills the book. Malachi faults them for bringing blind and lame beasts to the altar and warns them to give God due honor. Readers close the prophetic set with brisk debate about lax worship, hard times, and a great day still to come.
the-boy-allies-at-jutland-or-the-greates:
