Ensign Robert L. Drake wrote The Boy Allies at Jutland, or The Greatest Naval Battle of History, dated 1917. Drake had five more sea books in the set before it, among them The Boy Allies Under the Sea and The Boy Allies in the Baltic. The first chapter is named for H.M.S. Queen Mary.

A great, long, gray ship moves swift through the Thames as dusk falls. Smoke pours from three stacks and drifts west on the wind. Hours back she left her dock, where slight repairs had been done, and now heads east down the river. Men line her rails, and crowds throng both shores to cheer her off. Sharp orders ring out, men hurry to their posts, and her siren blasts. Then her speed grows, cheers rise from both banks, and the giant ship is lost in the dark.
the-mule-a-treatise-on-the-breeding-trai:
Harvey Riley's The Mule, a treatise on the breeding, training, and uses of the animal, was written in 1867 by the superintendent of the government corral at Washington, D.C. Its preface, dated April 12, 1867, calls the mule the most useful and willing of animals, and perhaps the most abused and least cared for.

Riley argues from thirty years of experience that kind treatment is what the mule most needs, and that kindness serves humanity and economy alike. He urges the government to employ only teamsters trained in managing animals, certified by the Quartermaster's Department. Such a system, he writes, would check the destruction of animal life that cost the government heavily every year.
the-night-before-christmas-and-other-pop:
The Night Before Christmas and Other Popular Stories for Children, handsomely illustrated as its title page boasts, was copyrighted in 1903 by the W. B. Conkey Company of Chicago. Only a title page, a contents list added by the transcriber, and the heading of the first story are present here, so the tales themselves do not appear. No editor or author is named for the collection as a whole.

Sixteen pieces are listed. The title poem heads them, followed by The Night After Christmas and Santa Claus Does Not Forget. The Fairy Christmas, The Dolls' Christmas Party, and Grandma's Christmas Gifts fill the middle. One heading is printed A Turkey Foe One, exactly as it stands in the list shown.
the-olden-time-series-vol-3-new-england-: New England Sunday is volume 3 of the Olden Time Series prepared by Henry M. Brooks, gleanings from old Boston and Salem newspapers with his brief comments. Only the publisher's series pages and the start of the title page are present here, so the Sunday pieces themselves do not appear. The same series pages open the other Olden Time volumes in this group. A quoted line calls Sunday the golden clasp that binds together the volume of the week.
the-world-s-greatest-books-volume-11-anc: Volume eleven of The World's Greatest Books, edited by Arthur Mee and J. A. Hammerton, covers ancient and medieval history in its contents list. Maspero's works on Egypt open the volume. Josephus supplies Jewish history, with his Antiquities and Wars. Herodotus and Thucydides represent Greece. Grote's History of Greece and Schliemann's Troy also appear. The history summaries themselves do not appear in the pages present here.
wanderings-among-south-sea-savages-and-i:
H. Wilfrid Walker, a fellow of the Royal Geographical Society, published his Wanderings among South Sea peoples and in Borneo and the Philippines in 1909. Witherby and Company issued it at London, with forty-eight plates from photographs. He dedicated the record to his brother Charles, who took a deep interest in the travels. His preface begins with apologies he calls a sheer necessity.

Most of the book, Walker says, is copied word for word from private letters home. He wrote them in simple language, in Dayak or Negrito huts and in the depths of tropical forest. He kept them short, so they could be read with ease. He never meant to write a book. Customs, ornaments, and weapons thus get less space than they might. The work makes no claim to be scientific. It relates the more striking incidents of a wandering life, as one traveller lived them.
what-is-free-trade-an-adaptation-of-fred: The pages shown hold just the title page and the start of a contents list, with none of the essays. Emile Walter adapted Frederic Bastiat's economic writings for American readers as What Is Free Trade? Putnam printed it in New York in 1867. Walter signs himself simply as a worker. The listed chapters begin with plenty and scarcity. Next come blocks to wealth and the causes of wealth. A chapter on effort and result follows. Later listed topics include the balance of trade and heavy home taxes on goods.
